chunk-001:c002.proposition: Christianity should acknowledge divine hiddenness as a genuine problem because scripture itself authorizes serious protest over God's felt absence.

chunk-001:c005.proposition: God can be ubiquitously present yet personally encountered through incarnation, while human resistance can diminish awareness of that personal nearness.

chunk-001:c009.proposition: The crucified Christ reveals a trustworthy God who enters humanity's experience of divine absence and God-forsaken suffering rather than explaining it from a distance.

chunk-002:c002-01.proposition: The Christian narrative identifies Jesus as the divine person who bears creation's suffering and judges resurrection worth that cost.

chunk-002:c002-03.proposition: Christian theology cannot make God wholly incommunicable because the unity of God and Christ connects divine life directly with embodied human suffering.

chunk-002:c002-05.proposition: The Trinity grounds goodness in an eternal personal community of other-directed love, avoiding both divine arbitrariness and an external moral standard.

chunk-002:c002-07.proposition: Naturalism's blind indifference does not account for objective wrongness, whereas Christianity supplies a standard by which suffering can be condemned as genuinely evil.

chunk-003:chunk-003-candidate-07.proposition: Biblical moral development has a discernible shape in which God patiently regulates nonideal conditions while Jesus restores creation's intended moral order.

chunk-003:chunk-003-candidate-09.proposition: The cruciform Jesus narrative supplies the governing criterion for judging whether actions taken in Christianity's name represent moral progress or regression.
